description: We are students from the Duval country area in Jacksonville Florida.
summary:
Draw a box around a place you know. EmberAlert lets you see what NASA’s satellites detected there over the past few days, either on a map or on a globe you can rotate.

The bigger question is what a busy month looks like for that place when the satellites observing it change over time. I built a Calibration Lab that tests a way to put MODIS and VIIRS detections on a common scale using years and areas it hasn’t seen during training. With suitable historical data, the burning calendar shows which months tend to have the most hotspot activity and how a particular month compares with its own past. A labeled synthetic example lets visitors try that process today.

I built EmberAlert to help land managers, researchers, and response teams see where to look now and which parts of the year deserve closer attention.
details:
I wanted someone to be able to open EmberAlert and start with a place they know. You can search for a city, draw a boundary, or enter coordinates, then step through recent NASA FIRMS detections one day at a time. The same observations appear on a street map, satellite imagery, and a globe you can rotate. Click a hotspot and you can see when it was recorded, which satellite detected it, and how confident the detection was. You can also save an area watch that checks for new reports while the page is visible.

The part that took the most thought was figuring out what a change in the hotspot count actually means. VIIRS can detect smaller hot spots than MODIS, so changing sensors can change the count even over the same landscape. I built a Calibration Lab that uses Aqua MODIS as a reference, compares observations with matched clear-sky coverage, and fits a conversion for each month. It tests those conversions on years and geographic blocks held back from the fit. When the project’s checks pass, comparable VIIRS observations can fill eligible gaps in the MODIS record.

That history can then feed the burning calendar. I wanted an empty month to stay visible as a gap, because missing coverage affects what you can conclude. The calendar compares sufficiently observed months with the median for that same month in earlier years. Visitors can try the workflow with a labeled synthetic sample or supply their own historical data. For land managers and response teams, the aim is to make it easier to see where to check recent activity and when to prepare for a busier season.

I built the interface with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. A Node.js endpoint retrieves and checks the NASA files, and Leaflet, Canvas, and MapLibre handle the map views. I used ChatGPT Sites for the first prototype, Codex to help implement and test revisions, GitHub for source control, and Vercel to publish the app. The guided tour points to controls visitors can try on the spot, while Advanced mode gives researchers access to calibration reports, source details, and exports.
